tasks.prompt: Compare wāt and wiste; cann and cūðe; gǣð and ēode; dēð and dyde. Using a third-person singular subject, identify the tense of each. Which forms can also serve a first-person singular subject? Explain why wāt and cann are not translated as past-tense forms.

tasks.prompt: The reference notes mark some modal infinitive citations as unattested or uncertain. Explain why a dictionary label such as mugan does not authorize you to create an infinitive or a command for every modal verb. Distinguish a missing paradigm cell from two attested cells with the same spelling.
tasks.target_specification: Defectiveness and evidence limits, without invented cells.

tasks.prompt: Translate “I know how to swim. We know how to sing.” Use cunnan for learned ability.
tasks.target_specification: Learned ability, present singular/plural; plain infinitives.
candidate_sequences: Ic cann swimman. Wē cunnon singan.

tasks.prompt: Translate “He can carry the water. They can help the man.” Use mugan for ability.
tasks.target_specification: Present ability; accusative carried object and dative helped person.
candidate_sequences: Hē mæg ðæt wæter beran. Hīe magon ðǣm męnn helpan.

tasks.prompt: Translate “I need to go. We needed to go.” Use ðurfan.
tasks.target_specification: Need with a plain infinitive; present and preterite.
candidate_sequences: Ic ðearf gān. Wē ðorfton gān.

tasks.prompt: Translate “You dare to go. You dared to go.” Address one person and use durran.
tasks.target_specification: Daring with a plain infinitive and explicit second-person singular.
candidate_sequences: Ðū dearst gān. Ðū dorstest gān.

tasks.prompt: Translate “We must do the work. They had to do the work.” Use sculan for obligation.
tasks.target_specification: Present and past obligation, not future or conditional projection.
candidate_sequences: Wē sculon ðæt weorc dōn. Hīe sceoldon ðæt weorc dōn.

tasks.prompt: Translate “You are allowed to eat the food. You were allowed to eat the food.” Address one person and use mōtan.
tasks.target_specification: Present and past permission; modal sense must be evidence-checked.
candidate_sequences: Ðū mōst ðone męte etan. Ðū mōstest ðone męte etan.

tasks.prompt: Translate “He wants to give the birds water. They wanted to give the birds water.” Use willan for desire.
tasks.target_specification: Volition with plain infinitive and prior giving frame.
candidate_sequences: Hē wille ðǣm fuglum wæter giefan. Hīe woldon ðǣm fuglum wæter giefan.

tasks.prompt: Translate “I did not dare to go. We cannot carry the ship.” Use the taught simple ne construction.
tasks.target_specification: Simple negation with audited irregular indicative systems; no negative concord or new contracted forms.
candidate_sequences: Ic ne dorste gān. Wē ne magon ðæt scip beran.

tasks.prompt: Translate “We two know how to swim. You two must help us two.” Keep the two-person references.
tasks.target_specification: Dual pronoun subjects with plural modal verbs and dative dual helped recipients.
candidate_sequences: Wit cunnon swimman. Git sculon unc helpan.

tasks.prompt: Translate “He wanted to go. He went.” Explain why the first sentence alone does not assert that he went.
tasks.target_specification: Volition distinguished from fulfilled motion, not mechanical future-in-the-past.
candidate_sequences: Hē wolde gān. Hē ēode.

tasks.prompt: Translate the printed pairs Ic cann swimman and Ic mæg swimman using the unit’s stated difference between learned ability and present capability. Identify the finite verb and the infinitive in each. Do not claim that one English word always represents only one Old English modal.
tasks.target_specification: Bounded modal contrast and finite versus nonfinite roles.
candidate_sequences: Ic cann swimman. Ic mæg swimman.

tasks.prompt: Translate “The ship will be ready.” Use the bēo-series indicative to describe the expected later state. Then contrast the earlier eom-series sentence “The ship is ready.” Do not infer that every bēo-series occurrence must be future.
tasks.target_specification: Elementary future-state bēon use with prior neuter predicate-adjective agreement; distinguish an assigned use from a universal tense rule.
candidate_sequences: Ðæt scip bið gearu. Ðæt scip is gearu.

tasks.prompt: The “things” here are matters already discussed. Translate “I know those things. He knew those things.” Use witan. Explain how this knowledge construction differs from cunnan followed by an infinitive.
tasks.target_specification: Present/past knowledge with an accusative nominal object and the prior pointing demonstrative; distinct from learned ability plus an infinitive.
candidate_sequences: Ic wāt ðā ðing. Hē wiste ðā ðing.

tasks.prompt: Translate “Do not drink the water. Sit and eat.” Address several people.

tasks.prompt: Translate “The man came to give food to the birds.” Use the inflected infinitive for the purpose.

tasks.prompt: In Hīe sculon ðæt weorc dōn and Hīe cōmon tō dōnne ðæt weorc, identify each finite verb, each infinitive, and the construction that selects the infinitive form. Translate both sentences.

candidate_sequences: Hīe sculon ðæt weorc dōn. Hīe cōmon tō dōnne ðæt weorc.

tasks.prompt: Complete the taught modal construction “We can carry the food” using mugan and beran. Then make the subject “I”. Explain which verb changes for person and number.
tasks.target_specification: Only the finite modal agrees; the plain infinitive remains unchanged.
candidate_sequences: Wē magon ðone męte beran. Ic mæg ðone męte beran.

tasks.prompt: Read “Food and water for the journey”. Who asks for help, how many companions come, and what is their stated purpose? Answer in English.
tasks.target_specification: Actor/number/purpose from the controlled text.

tasks.prompt: List every imperative in the controlled text and give its addressee number. For each, give the singular command form taught in the tables.
tasks.target_specification: Plural imperative recognition and singular production across the connected instructions.

tasks.prompt: In the controlled text, identify the antecedent and case of hine, the recipient of the water, and what the companions subsequently eat. Distinguish what is explicit from what the context suggests.
tasks.target_specification: Grammatical reference and bounded contextual inference; no uniquely encoded final hīe antecedent demanded.

tasks.prompt: Identify wille, mæg and sculon in the controlled text by person, number, tense and stated sense. Give the infinitive governed by each.
tasks.target_specification: Three finite modal/volitional clauses and their plain infinitives.

tasks.prompt: Translate the whole controlled text. Preserve the distinctions among a wish to travel, ability to carry, obligation, commands and completed past actions.
tasks.target_specification: Complete independent translation from exact Old English with no extra event claims.

tasks.prompt: Rewrite the man’s first quoted commands, Cumað and helpað mē, as commands to one companion. Then put the first sentence of the narrative into the present, keeping the quotation itself unchanged.
tasks.target_specification: Number adjustment in commands and finite narrative-tense adjustment with stable quotation.
candidate_sequences: Cum and help mē. Se mann cwið: ‘Ic wille faran. Mīn scip is gearu. Cumað and helpað mē.’

tasks.prompt: Read “The fisherman’s gift and first direction”, using its local support. What prompts the fisherman’s action, what does he divide, and what does he give Apollonius?
tasks.target_specification: Source event sequence; the local supports remain visible.

tasks.prompt: Find wolde and its plain infinitive in the source. Parse wolde and explain the fisherman’s intention. Use the supplied meaning of gecȳðan.
tasks.target_specification: Past volition plus an explicitly supplied lexical infinitive.

tasks.prompt: Identify tō bēodanne and tō sęllanne. Give the familiar plain infinitive behind each. Explain the source’s “have to offer/give” phrases using the printed support; do not translate them as modern English “must”.
tasks.target_specification: Inflected infinitive forms and source-specific available-to-offer construction.

tasks.prompt: Find the source’s two singular commands. Parse each and give its plural command form from the taught system.
tasks.target_specification: Nim and gā as actual second-person commands, with productive plural equivalents.

tasks.prompt: Use the notes to distinguish the participial cweðende from the finite past cwæð and the command gā. Which form introduces the fisherman’s actual words?
tasks.target_specification: Supplied participle recognition without productive participial syntax.

tasks.prompt: What does the fisherman say he has, and what first direction does he give? Explain the force of the phrase translated “what I have” using the local support.
tasks.target_specification: Gift and direction; free-relative support remains supplied.

tasks.prompt: Identify the source’s tō phrases that contain an inflected infinitive and distinguish them from tō his hūse and intō ðǣre ceastre. State the locally supplied meanings of the destination phrases without deriving a general motion-preposition rule.
tasks.target_specification: Infinitive marker versus supplied destination phrases; exact case preserved.

tasks.prompt: Translate the whole 76-word source excerpt with its supports. Stop after the fisherman’s first direction; do not add the continuation of his speech.
tasks.target_specification: Complete exact-span translation and transparent excerpt boundary.

tasks.prompt: Translate “We two wanted to give our food to the birds. We two gave it to them.” Retain the two-person possessor and the grammatical gender of “food”.
tasks.target_specification: Cumulative dual reference, agreeing possessive, volitional infinitive, past giving and anaphora.
candidate_sequences: Wit woldon uncerne męte ðǣm fuglum giefan. Wit gēafon hine him.

tasks.prompt: Translate “The old man cannot carry the great ship. Help him.” Address several companions in the command.
tasks.target_specification: Weak attributive adjectives, modal negation, accusative object and dative help-recipient.
candidate_sequences: Se ealda mann ne mæg ðæt micle scip beran. Helpað him.

tasks.prompt: Translate “He came to help us. We wanted to give him food. He sat and ate.” Use the taught elementary purpose and volitional constructions.
tasks.target_specification: Purpose, desire, dative recipients and completed indicative actions.
candidate_sequences: Hē cōm tō helpanne ūs. Wē woldon him męte giefan. Hē sæt and ǣt.

tasks.prompt: Compare the statement Gē gāð with the command Gāð. Explain the shared spelling and the difference in use. Then compare Hē dēð ðæt weorc with Dō ðæt weorc.
tasks.target_specification: Syncretism does not erase mood/use distinctions; singular imperative differs from indicative3sg.
candidate_sequences: Gē gāð. Gāð. Hē dēð ðæt weorc. Dō ðæt weorc.

tasks.prompt: Write four connected Old English sentences about a man and two companions: one past arrival with an explicitly stated purpose, one statement of willingness, one direct command addressed to both companions, and one completed past action. Use cuman, helpan, willan and beran, with mann, gefēra and męte and any needed taught articles or pronouns. Label the three new constructions.
tasks.target_specification: Controlled open composition with an explicit lexical bank and audited frames; key supplies a defensible model without reducing validity to one string.
